newsitem.title: USA: Jurors urged to punish Simpson with heavy damages.
newsitem.headline: Jurors urged to punish Simpson with heavy damages.

text.p: The plaintiffs' lead attorney in O.J. Simpson's civil trial urged jurors on Friday to impose stiff punitive damages against him to send a message that "You cannot kill two people and get away with it."

In an impassioned closing argument in the final phase of the four-month trial, attorney Daniel Petrocelli told jurors: "You are the last ones who will have the power to reach out and punish him for what he did."
Pointing out Simpson's absence from court on Friday, Petrocelli implored jurors to "send him a message so loud that he can hear it on whatever golf course he is hiding out on right now."
The jury on Tuesday blamed Simpson for the 1994 murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman, and awarded $8.5 million in damages to Goldman's divorced parents.

The plaintiffs now want the jury to punish him further by awarding millions more to the estates of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman. Simpson was cleared of murder charges in in October 1995 but the victims' families pressed ahead with a wrongful-death lawsuit in civil court. Jurors could begin deliberating punitive damages by Friday afternoon.

As the trial neared an end, Petrocelli, who represented the Goldman family, looked directly at the jury and in a loud, booming voice, declared: "You must send him a message that ... you cannot kill two people and get away with it no matter how much money you have, no matter how many lies you tell."

Earlier, jurors were told Simpson is unable to earn any money and is struggling to pay his bills. Leroy "Skip" Taft, Simpson's business manager, said Simpson's current earning capacity was nil and his future prospects were bleak.
Taft, a defence witness, gave the jurors a glimpse of what it costs to live in the world of the rich and famous, listing Simpson's considerable monthly expenses.
He said the mortgage on Simpson's mansion in the posh Brentwood section of Los Angeles was $24,000 a month "when he pays it," and maintenance was another $30,000 a month.

In addition, Taft said in answer to questions from plaintiffs' attorney Peter Gelblum, he charged the former athlete about $10,000 a month for his services; Simpson pays his personal secretary $3,000 a month and employs a full-time bodyguard, whose salary was not disclosed.
Simpson recently bought a $54,000 Chevrolet Suburban and owns a Bentley worth between $35,000 and $40,000, Taft said.
He also told the jury Simpson owes him thousands of dollars in unpaid fees which he did not expect to ever receive. "He has to pay his bills selectively," Taft said.

When Gelblum suggested that a condominium in San Francisco where Simpson's elderly, wheelchair-bound mother lives would revert to him after her death, his sister, Shirley Baker, muttered an obscenity and stormed out of the courtroom.

Taft said Simpson's recent efforts to exploit his name had met with no success. Promoters of sports memorabilia shows refused to have Simpson and the only promoter who accepted him for a show cancelled after receiving bomb threats.

Neill Freeman, an accountant and financial investigator testifying for the plaintiffs on Thursday, said Simpson was far from being broke and had a net worth of more than $15.7 million. He said Simpson had future earning potential for the rest of his life of about $24.9 million by cashing in on his notoriety with product endorsements and autograph signings.
But Taft disputed both figures, saying it was "ludicrous" to say that Simpson could earn such sums in the future.
Marvin Goodfriend, an accountant called by the defence, said it was "highly speculative" to talk about future earnings when Simpson did not have a single contract.
